title: MLflow for GenAI
subtitle: Tracing, evaluation and observability
notes: Lecture 4. We build on the arXiv agent from lecture 3. Today focuses on tracing. Experiment tracking and model registration prepare the Model Serving demonstration next week.

title: Agenda
rows: Regular ML, GenAI and Unity Catalog
Test behavior, define scorers and inspect failures
Prepare an agent for Model Serving

title: MLflow components
rows: Main use: machine learning. Compare training runs, parameters, metrics and artifacts.
Manage model versions and aliases in Unity Catalog. Share models across workspaces.
Understand what happens inside an agent. OpenTelemetry-compatible and closely tied to evaluation.
bottom: For an agent behind a Model Serving endpoint, also log the agent and register a model version.
notes: A run records an experiment execution or evaluation. A trace records a request and its spans. A registered model version identifies an artifact for reuse or deployment. These objects are related but have different purposes. MLflow tracing was introduced in MLflow 2.14.0 in June 2024. For the Model Serving workflow demonstrated next week, log the agent in an MLflow run and register it in Unity Catalog. Databricks Apps remains our recommended application route.

title: LLM observability tools also support evaluation
bottom: This comparison maps to MLflow tracing and evaluation.
notes: This capability overview covers observability and evaluation, not feature parity. MLflow also provides experiment tracking and a model registry. Human review and feedback are supported by MLflow, Phoenix and Opik. Langfuse also provides tracing, evaluation and human annotation.

title: Model flavors and payloads
notes: Framework flavors package models; the deployed interface and model signature determine request and response schemas. ResponsesAgent uses a Responses-style schema, not a guarantee that every OpenAI Responses API feature is supported. DSPy and LangChain do not universally imply a chat payload. Transformers deployment depends on supported model families and architectures. Foundation model endpoint tasks include chat, embeddings and completions where supported. Tensor payloads use instances or inputs. The classic ML payload examples are alternatives, not one combined request. For Databricks, invoke the workspace serving endpoint; the OpenAI public API URL is not the deployment destination. Redrawn from the user-provided model flavors and payload visual.

title: Storage and governance
subtitle: Regular ML, GenAI and Unity Catalog

title: Regular ML and GenAI experiments
table: Workspace experiments: training runs, parameters and metrics
Experiments organize traces and evaluations; trace data can be stored in Unity Catalog
For Model Serving: log and register the agent in Unity Catalog
bottom: Model Serving is the overlap: log the agent in an MLflow run, then register it in Unity Catalog.
notes: Compare experiment use cases: regular ML training versus GenAI tracing and evaluation. These are workflows, not two separate underlying experiment object types. Experiment metadata is workspace scoped; UC-backed GenAI trace payloads use governed tables. In our regular ML setup, registered models are in UC. Agent deployment through Model Serving also uses an MLflow run and a UC registered model version. Experiment artifact storage can separately use a UC volume. Databricks Apps is our recommended course application route.

title: Why GenAI changes the data sensitivity
rows: Often log aggregate metrics and parameters. These can reveal less than the original training records.
Can capture full user queries, responses, retrieved documents and tool arguments.
A second copy of business data
Someone who can read the trace may see content from a protected source.
bottom: ML artifacts, samples and logged inputs can also contain sensitive data.
notes: The distinction is typical content, not a guarantee that traditional ML tracking is safe. Do not log secrets. Consider what inputs and outputs instrumentation captures, and minimize unnecessary payloads. This privacy motivation is the additional rationale requested for the lecture.

title: Workspace administration and trace access
rows: Workspace admins can manage experiment permissions and potentially read sensitive trace contents.
Trace access follows UC data privileges. We can give application teams access to their own trace data.
Use a governed catalog with deliberate ownership and grants. UC does not automatically exclude every administrator.
bottom: A workspace admin may also hold UC privileges or be able to grant access.
notes: Workspace admins have CAN MANAGE on workspace objects. For UC, review catalog ownership, inherited grants and privileged roles. Workspace admins are default owners of an automatically provisioned workspace catalog and can grant themselves data access there. A separate governed catalog can support the desired separation. This is an access-control boundary, not a promise against all powerful administrators.

title: Registered models in Unity Catalog
rows: catalog.schema.arxiv_agent holds versions of the logged agent artifact.
Authorized users can access the model from workspaces attached to the same metastore, subject to catalog bindings.
Choose an explicit version for deployment. An alias is a movable reference to a version.
bottom: Model registration and trace storage are separate UC concerns.
notes: Model access requires the relevant privileges. Workspace-catalog bindings can further restrict access. Registering an agent does not deploy an endpoint or grant the agent access to its dependencies.

title: A trace records one execution
rows: The request-level record, including status, duration, identifiers and a collection of spans.
One operation, with a start/end time, inputs, outputs and attributes.
Nested spans preserve the relationship between the agent, model calls and tools.
bottom: A conversation can contain multiple request traces linked by a session ID.
notes: A span may represent an LLM call, retrieval or a tool invocation. The trace is the execution record, not a transcript alone. OpenTelemetry provides a common tracing model. Integration and payload details still matter when sending data to another backend.

title: One request through the arXiv agent
code:
predict_stream                         AGENT
  call_and_run_tools                   CHAIN
    memory_load                        RETRIEVER
    LLM call                           LLM
    execute_tool                       TOOL
      search_papers                    retrieval work
    LLM call                           LLM
    memory_save                        CHAIN
bottom: Illustrative hierarchy. Actual spans depend on the executed path and integrations.
notes: Based on src/arxiv_curator/agent.py. The current source uses RETRIEVER for memory_load, CHAIN for memory_save and TOOL for execute_tool. LLM spans require the appropriate instrumentation. Do not claim this is a captured production trace. Use the live demo to show the exact span tree.

title: What a trace helps us investigate
rows: Which span dominates the request? Is the agent making repeated tool calls?
What did retrieval return? What did the model receive? Did memory load the expected history?
How many model calls ran? Where available, compare token usage by span and version.
bottom: A successful trace status describes execution, not answer quality.
notes: Span durations can overlap, so summing child durations is not always equal to request latency. Token and cost data depend on instrumentation and model support. Separate evidence from hypotheses during debugging.

title: Instrumentation choices
rows: Use the integration for your model or framework to capture supported operations.
Instrument your own functions and choose meaningful span names and types.
Control the scope of a span and explicitly record inputs or outputs.
notes: Notebook 4.1 introduces decorators and manual spans. OpenTelemetry compatibility does not mean all frameworks record identical attributes or all backends accept every field. Avoid logging credentials in arguments or metadata.

title: UC trace setup
code:
from mlflow.entities.trace_location import UnityCatalog

experiment = mlflow.set_experiment(
    experiment_name=cfg.experiment_name,
    trace_location=UnityCatalog(
        catalog_name=cfg.catalog,
        schema_name=cfg.schema,
        table_prefix="llmops",
    ),
)
bottom: Notebook 4.0 verifies existing bindings and configures the application principal.
notes: Excerpt from notebooks/4.0.uc_traces_setup.py. Run the full notebook: it sets the warehouse ID, checks existing experiment bindings and grants access. The catalog and schema must already exist. The current docs require MLflow 3.14 or later for this UC workflow. Do not interpret this excerpt as all required setup.

title: Permissions and deployment checks
rows: Give each identity the privileges needed for its task. Check inherited access as well as direct grants.
Notebook 4.0 grants the service principal SELECT and MODIFY on trace tables, and SELECT on views.
Generate a trace with the application identity, then verify that an intended reader can inspect it.
bottom: Experiment access alone does not grant access to UC trace payloads.
notes: The course notebook assumes necessary parent USE CATALOG and USE SCHEMA grants already exist. Table-level SELECT, MODIFY and view SELECT grants do not grant these parent privileges. Use a dedicated trace destination where possible and review the notebook prefix-based object selection. Check SQL warehouse access for readers. Validate both allowed access and denied access for an unrelated user. No permissions are changed by these slides.

title: A parent span and two child spans
bottom: Notebook 4.1 starts with simulated operations so the span structure is easy to inspect.
notes: Adapted from notebook 4.1. Imports and decorated child functions are defined earlier in the notebook. This excerpt illustrates nesting, not a complete application. A simulated LLM function is not a real model call.

title: Metadata connects requests to versions
bottom: Use real deployment identifiers. Avoid secrets and unnecessary personal data.
notes: Adapted from notebook 4.1. Call within an active trace. request_id identifies one client request, session_id groups related turns, and git_sha/model_version identify implementation changes. Placeholder git SHAs in demonstrations must be replaced in real deployments.

title: Demo: inspect the agent execution
rows: Verify the UC destination, generate a simple trace, then inspect nested spans and metadata.
Ask for papers, then ask a follow-up using the same session ID.
Find the memory load, tool call and final response. Explain which evidence supports the answer.
bottom: ResponsesAgent packages prediction behavior. Tracing shows what that behavior did.
notes: Use notebooks/4.0.uc_traces_setup.py, 4.1.tracing_implementation.py and 4.2.custom_agent.py. Show src/arxiv_curator/agent.py only where it clarifies a span or prediction method. Keep tools and memory implementation brief because lecture 3 covered them. The user should be able to explain a trace, not memorize every agent method.

title: Evaluation
subtitle: Test behavior, define scorers and inspect failures

title: Evaluation data starts with expected behavior
rows: Start with a small, reviewed set of normal requests and meaningful edge cases.
Include prior turns or evidence when the task needs them. Record what a useful response must do.
Group failures, refine the criteria with domain reviewers, and keep regression cases.
bottom: For arXiv: paper evidence, topic relevance, follow-up context and honest uncertainty.
notes: For the exercise, consider starting with roughly 10–20 high-quality examples as a practical exercise, not a universal statistical requirement. Include absent evidence, unrelated requests and follow-up questions. A file with only questions is a starting point but does not encode per-example expectations. Keep a separate held-out set for comparing changes.

title: Metrics define what; scorers define how
bottom: A metric is the quality dimension. A scorer produces its assessment.
notes: Use multiple forms of evidence. Human disagreement can expose an ambiguous criterion rather than a model failure. Scorer outputs can be boolean, categorical or numeric.

title: MLflow scorers: choosing the evidence
bottom: Choose a scorer that can see the evidence needed for the judgment.
notes: These are selected examples, not the full API inventory. The Correctness row uses the common reference-based workflow; supported configurations can differ. Retrieval scorers require correctly instrumented retrieval information. A final-answer-only check cannot prove the agent used the right tool.

title: Guidelines and custom judges
rows: Apply shared natural-language criteria and assess pass/fail.
Define task-specific instructions, template inputs and a suitable output type.
A rule can flag a repeated suggestion. A custom judge can assess how well the agent acknowledges earlier attempts.
bottom: A more elaborate judge still needs comparison with human feedback.
notes: Uniform Guidelines apply across evaluation rows. Use per-example expectations where the expected behavior changes. make_judge supports inputs, outputs, expectations and trace-based assessment. A numeric scale is useful only when each grade has a clear meaning.

title: A guideline for conversation context
code:
from mlflow.genai.scorers import Guidelines

context_guideline = Guidelines(
    name="acknowledges_previous_attempts",
    guidelines=[
        "If the user says earlier attempts failed, acknowledge "
        "those attempts and offer a new approach or escalation."
    ],
    model=JUDGE_MODEL,
)
bottom: Include the relevant conversation in the evaluation input.
notes: JUDGE_MODEL is the configured judge endpoint. A guideline cannot evaluate hidden conversation history that it never receives. Avoid applying this criterion to standalone questions without its conditional wording.

title: A custom judge with an explicit rubric
code:
from mlflow.genai.judges import make_judge

context_judge = make_judge(
    name="context_handling",
    instructions=(
        "Given {{ inputs }} and {{ outputs }}, score 1–3: "
        "1 = repeats a failed suggestion; "
        "2 = acknowledges failure but gives no useful next step; "
        "3 = acknowledges failure and offers a relevant next step."
    ),
    feedback_value_type=int, model=JUDGE_MODEL,
)
bottom: Review disagreements against the rubric before using the score for decisions.
notes: Teaching adaptation of a conversation-context example. This is an illustrative 1–3 rubric. The integer type alone does not enforce that every model response falls in the requested range. Inspect the returned feedback and validate the judge with reviewed examples.

title: Our course scorers: useful but incomplete
rows: Checks whether the response is under 350 words.
Assess tone and whether the response starts with an engaging opening.
A short, polite post can still misrepresent a paper. Add factual support and task-specific expectations.
bottom: The mentions_papers keyword check also cannot establish factual correctness.
notes: Source: src/arxiv_curator/evaluation.py. Notebook 4.4 runs word_count_check, polite_tone_guideline and hook_in_post_guideline. scope_guideline and mentions_papers exist but are not in that evaluation call. Hook criteria should apply to post-writing tasks, not automatically every response. This is an intentional teaching discussion of the limits of the existing demonstration.

title: Demo: evaluate and inspect a failure
code:
results = mlflow.genai.evaluate(
    predict_fn=predict_fn,
    data=eval_data,
    scorers=[
        word_count_check,
        polite_tone_guideline,
        hook_in_post_guideline,
    ],
)
bottom: Notebooks 4.3–4.4: read the output, scorer rationale and underlying trace together.
notes: Excerpt from notebook 4.4. predict_fn takes question and returns the agent output. eval_data maps each question to an inputs dictionary. Start with a passing example and then inspect a failure or a false pass. Explain what the scorer actually checked and what it could not establish.

title: Judge reliability needs human calibration
rows: Give reviewers and the judge the same criteria and relevant context.
Inspect false passes and false failures. Clarify ambiguous rules and missing evidence.
Reassess on examples that were not used to refine the judge.
bottom: LLM judges provide scalable feedback, not an unquestionable ground truth.
notes: Keep advanced statistical judge replacement tests and automated alignment outside the main lecture. The purpose here is practical calibration and avoiding evaluation overfitting.

title: Tracking and registration
subtitle: Prepare an agent for Model Serving

title: Tracking and registration complete the workflow
rows: Inspect individual cases and aggregate metrics. Decide whether the version is ready.
Record evaluation metrics in an MLflow run and log the configured agent artifact.
Create a UC model version and update an alias deliberately. Deploy the chosen version next week.
bottom: Logging metrics does not automatically enforce a release gate.
notes: Notebook 4.4 evaluates, logs the agent, logs results.metrics, registers the model, and sets latest-model. The notebook does not implement a pass/fail release gate. It also uses placeholder git_sha/run_id values, which should be replaced for production provenance. We do not claim the existing notebook blocks bad versions.

title: The agent artifact for next week
code:
with mlflow.start_run(run_name="arxiv-agent"):
    model_info = mlflow.pyfunc.log_model(
        name="agent", python_model=agent,
        input_example=test_request, model_config=model_config,
    )
    mlflow.log_metrics(results.metrics)

registered_model = mlflow.register_model(
    model_uri=model_info.model_uri,
    name=f"{cfg.catalog}.{cfg.schema}.arxiv_agent",
)
bottom: Notebook 4.4 contains the complete registration and alias configuration.
notes: Simplified excerpt from notebook 4.4. The full notebook passes env_pack at registration. It logs an initialized ResponsesAgent and does not configure automatic resource-based authentication. The Model Serving demonstration must configure the dedicated service principal credentials and required resource access, including trace access. Do not put credential values in model_config. Apps remains our recommended course application route.

title: Production observability
subtitle: Evaluate live traffic and prevent regressions

title: System lifecycle starts after deployment
notes: The confidence curves are conceptual, not measured performance. Connect them to changing user questions and retrieved content. Deployment starts the production observation period.

title: Monitoring vs observability
notes: Monitoring detects known symptoms such as latency or error rates. Observability supplies the evidence needed to investigate unexpected behavior. A user report can reveal a problem even when operational indicators look healthy.

title: Easy checks can miss a real problem
notes: Ask students whether this response deserves a passing score. Politeness and length can pass while the response ignores the previous conversation. These are illustrative results in this example, not benchmark measurements.

title: Evaluate the response in context
notes: Compare the returning issue, quick question and repeated suggestion. A clarification may be appropriate for a new question and frustrating when the user has already supplied the context. Trace evidence shows whether the system loaded or retrieved that context.

title: Observability and evaluation work together
notes: Evaluation identifies an unsatisfactory response. Inspect the trace to distinguish missing retrieval, a memory problem, or failure to use available context. Add the observed failure to the evaluation set.

title: Tiered evaluation in production
notes: The rates and cadence are illustrative. Cheap checks may run in application code or a scheduled job. Current MLflow automatic evaluation supports LLM judges, while custom code-based scorers are for offline evaluation. See https://mlflow.org/docs/latest/genai/eval-monitor/scorers/custom/

title: Production failures become regression cases
rows: Combine operational signals with feedback and sampled quality assessments.
Inspect the affected traces and identify the failure mechanism.
Add the case to evaluation data, change the agent, and compare versions before release.
bottom: Protect trace access and retention throughout the feedback loop.
notes: Keep development evaluations and live monitoring connected through a versioned failure taxonomy. Monitor collection gaps as well as application quality. Evaluation samples need coverage of rare but consequential failures.

title: Homework: trace, evaluate and explain
rows: Configure its trace destination. Show a request with meaningful spans and version/session metadata.
Create a small reviewed dataset. Add a code check and a domain-specific judge with clear expectations.
Attach a sanitized trace example, explain the failure, and add a regression case.
Open a pull request with the implementation, evaluation findings and intended trace permissions.
notes: Use notebooks 4.0–4.4 as the reference. Include at least a normal request, missing-evidence case, unrelated request and follow-up question. Do not commit raw sensitive traces or secrets. Registration is useful preparation for the optional Model Serving route next week. Ask students to explain who can read the traces and why.
